explanation.whatDescription: A transit happens when a satellite (ISS or Tiangong) passes exactly between you and the Sun or Moon: it then appears as a dark silhouette on the disk, usually for less than a second in front of the Sun (a bit longer in front of the closer Moon).

params.angularSize: The satellite's apparent size in the sky, in arcseconds.
params.position: The direction (azimuth) and height (altitude) to look at during the transit.
params.duration: The time the satellite takes to cross the disk.
params.missDistance: How close the satellite passes to the disk's center.

details.eyeSafety: Never look at the Sun without a certified solar filter (ND5), even during the transit: the satellite doesn't reduce the radiation at all.

groundPath.title: Visibility line
groundPath.hint: Each point on the line corresponds to a different moment of the pass: moving along the band shifts the transit time slightly rather than showing it everywhere at once. Indicative position (accurate to within a few kilometers, cruder for a lunar transit).
